question: What safety and accessibility priority does the MUTCD establish for temporary traffic control planning and operation?
model_answer: Direct Answer: The MUTCD establishes that road user and worker safety and accessibility should be an integral, high-priority element of every project involving temporary traffic control, from planning through design and construction. This priority extends to all motorists, bicyclists, pedestrians (including those with disabilities), and workers at all times, and TTC operations should minimize inconvenience, delay, and crash potential to affected traffic. These are Guidance (recommended) provisions; no mandatory Standard on this priority appears in the evidence. Guidance (recommended): - "Road user and worker safety and accessibility in TTC zones should be an integral and high-priority element of every project from planning through design and construction. Similarly, maintenance and utility work should be planned and conducted with the safety and accessibility of all motorists, bicyclists, pedestrians (including those with disabilities), and workers being considered at all times. If the TTC zone includes a grade crossing, early coordination with the railroad company or light rail transit agency should take place." - The seven fundamental principles of TTC include: general plans or guidelines should be developed to provide safety for motorists, bicyclists, pedestrians, workers, and enforcement/emergency officials; the basic safety principles governing permanent roadway design should also govern TTC zone design; a TTC plan appropriate to the project's complexity should be prepared and understood by all responsible parties before the site is occupied; and road user movement should be inhibited as little as practical. - "Temporary traffic control operations should minimize the inconvenience, delay, and crash potential to affected traffic. Prior notice should be given to affected public or private agencies, emergency services, businesses, railroad companies or transit agencies, and road users before the free movement of road users or rail traffic is infringed upon or blocked." Support (context, non-normative): - When the normal function of the roadway is suspended, TTC planning provides for continuity of movement of motor vehicle, bicycle, and pedestrian traffic (including accessible passage), transit operations, and access (and accessibility) to property and utilities. - Temporary traffic control planning at grade crossings similarly provides for continuity of operations, including pedestrian and bicyclist movement and access to property/utilities. - The overall purpose of the MUTCD is to establish uniform national criteria for traffic control devices that meet the needs and expectancy of road users on all facilities, including pedestrian and bicycle facilities. Visual evidence: [Image 6] shows the full text of Section 6A.02 "Fundamental Principles of Temporary Traffic Control," including the high-priority safety and accessibility Guidance in paragraph 01 and the seven fundamental principles in paragraph 02. [Image 8] shows Section 8A.13 "Temporary Traffic Control Zones," including the Guidance that TTC operations should minimize inconvenience, delay, and crash potential to affected traffic. [Image 5] shows the table of contents for Part 6, confirming Chapter 6C is devoted to "Pedestrian and Worker Safety," including accessibility considerations. [Image 7] shows Section 6L.01, whose Support notes that accessible pedestrian signals provide non-visual information so pedestrians with vision disabilities can cross safely along an alternate route in TTC zones. Citations: - Section 6A.02 Guidance §1 (p.766) - Section 6A.02 Guidance §2 (p.768) - Section 8A.13 Guidance §7 (p.992) - Section 6A.01 Support §3 (p.765) - Section 8A.13 Support §1 (p.992) - Section 1A.01 Support §1 (p.1) - Page 807 - Page 1033 - Page 22 - Page 865
gold_answer: Road-user and worker safety and accessibility must be treated as integral, high-priority considerations from planning through design and construction, including motorists, bicyclists, pedestrians with disabilities, workers, and coordination with rail transit where applicable.
